The framework

Five decisions, in the order that saves you money

Everything a foreign founder needs to settle before capital is paid in. Each layer has a stop condition: hit one and the plan ends, which is usually the cheapest possible outcome.

  1. 1FitDoes your business need a Chinese entity at all?

How to use this

Read the five layers in order, once, before you register anything. It takes about forty minutes. Then use the layer that matches where you actually are — most founders discover they are on layer four while still undecided about layer one.

01

Does your business need a Chinese entity at all?

Most founders register a company before they can say what the company is for. Start with the job the entity has to do — invoice, hire, hold a licence, or nothing yet.

Fit 02

Are you allowed to do this, here?

The negative list, the sector licence and the registered address decide whether a company is possible at all — before structure, capital or tax matter.

Access 03

Which vehicle, and who controls it?

WFOE, joint venture, representative office or a Hong Kong holding company: four different answers to control, liability, tax and the exit you will need one day.

Structure 04

How much capital, and how does money move?

Registered capital is a promise with a five-year clock. The bank account, the capital account and the invoice system decide whether you can actually trade.

Money 05

Who runs it, and how does it stay legal?

Work permits, payroll, social insurance, annual filings, audit and the closure you will eventually need. A company is a recurring obligation, not a one-off filing.

Continuity

The stop conditions

What ends a plan, and at which layer

These are the situations where the correct answer is to stop. Reading them first is faster than learning them at a bank counter.

Layer 1 — Fit

  • The activity is prohibited to foreign investment and your plan is a nominee shareholder or a VIE.
  • The licence you need is not available to a foreign-owned entity in your city, and no permitted structure exists.
  • You cannot name a single customer who will pay the Chinese entity.

Layer 2 — Access

  • Your only route to market is invoicing through a Chinese friend's company.
  • You are about to sign a lease before the environmental, fire or sector approval that the site depends on.
  • The registered address is a virtual address that the bank has already refused, or that no landlord will document.

Layer 3 — Structure

  • The business depends on bringing client money through the company without a payment licence.
  • The registered capital you need for the licence is money you do not have and cannot raise within five years.
  • Your Chinese partner's contribution is 'relationships' with no contract, no valuation and no exit mechanism.

Layer 4 — Money

  • You plan to be the legal representative but will not live in China or employ a local manager with authority.
  • Your product handles personal data at a scale you have not mapped, and you have no data-compliance plan.
  • The only person who can operate the business is a foreign national who does not qualify for a work permit.

Layer 5 — Continuity

  • You are relying on a verbal assurance from an official that a licence 'will be fine'.
  • Your budget covers registration but not the first twelve months of losses.
  • You have not read the articles of association or the joint-venture contract you are about to sign.
